brief.head: Save for a rainy year
brief.text: Ajay Shah’s rule for fiscal policy: run a small primary balance every year and be non-discretionary, saving room for large deficits in a 2008-style crisis or pandemic. {041-C05}

brief.head: Money from thin air
brief.text: A central bank makes money out of thin air, Ajay Shah said, “just like the Bitcoin and Ethereum folk do”. It then sets the overnight interest rate. {041-J09}

brief.head: Friends who differ
brief.text: Hayek’s great rival was Keynes, yet the biographer of both found Hayek personally closer to Keynes than to his ally Friedman. Amit Varma loves that friends can disagree. {041-S05}

brief.head: Shaped by war and flu
brief.text: Friedrich Hayek fought in the First World War, where an attack in 1917 damaged part of the hearing in his left ear. In 1918 he survived the Spanish flu. {041-S03}

brief.head: Nobody designed it
brief.text: Languages evolve with no central committee, and natural selection made humans and trees with no planner, Amit Varma said. “There’s no God, though that is the subject for another day.” {041-J10}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the papers that shaped them
lead.head: Small print, big ideas
body: People think of papers as boring, Amit Varma said at the start of the episode. He and Ajay Shah set out to prove otherwise, with papers they consider seminal, thrilling and well written, and which, Varma said, crafted the modern world.
They promised five. They delivered four, three papers and an essay, and Varma later explained the shortfall: “Because the light is going down.” {041-J05}
Two picks were Shah’s and two Varma’s, running from a French essay of the middle of the nineteenth century to an American speech of 1968.
## The reading list
Shah began with Milton Friedman’s *The Role of Monetary Policy*, which appeared in 1968. {041-R01}

Of the thousands of macroeconomics papers he has read, he said, this is the one that lights up the journey of the twentieth century. It treats people as optimisers who respond to government, and keeps monetary policy to one modest job: stable prices.
Varma followed with Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, which, admitting his bias, he called the greatest work of the twentieth century. {041-R02}
Its argument is that knowledge is scattered across millions of people and changes all the time, so no planner can ever gather it. Prices do the coordinating instead.

Shah’s second pick was Ronald Coase’s 1937 article *The Nature of the Firm*. It asks why the economy runs on bargaining outside firms and on obedience inside them, and answers that contracting is costly.

Varma closed with Frédéric Bastiat’s essay *That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen*, which gave his podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, its name. Its broken window, he said, taught opportunity cost about sixty years before the term was coined.
## Against the all-knowing
A distrust of the all-knowing ran through the conversation.
Shah described the Keynesian paradigm that Friedman overturned as one in which the policymakers “are wise and all-knowing” and the people “are more or less dumb”.
Varma saw a similar conceit in people drunk on power, with their “engineering mindset that we can design this”. A lot of the time, he said, the state just needs to get out of the way.
Even within companies, Shah argued, power works better dispersed. The great firms are institutions that outlast their chief executives.
Prices moved both hosts. “When you pause to think about it, we are moved to rapture,” Shah said.
## Ways of thinking

What lasts, Varma argued, is less any paper’s conclusion than the frame of thought behind it. “I think every great paper of economics is teaching us how to think about life and live our lives better,” he said. {041-C15}

For newcomers, Shah recommended Tyler Cowen’s *GOAT* as an ideal starting point on Friedman, Hayek and Keynes. Varma recommended Marginal Revolution University, whose videos, he said, are basically recorded PowerPoints.
Then Varma offered a final thought. Bastiat, Hayek and Friedman are no more, he said, but ideas are what shape civilisation.
“One day, Ajay and I will also be gone,” he said, before wondering why it had to be someday: they could be gone now.
The next shot belonged to a little girl hosting a parody channel, *Nothing Is Nothing*. Shah suspected she had been playing with them all along. {041-J11}

second.label: Wittgenstein
second.head: Not a Tractatus in sight
second.deck: Amit Varma on what the great philosopher wrote in the First World War trenches
body: Friedrich Hayek, Amit Varma said, was the second cousin of Ludwig Wittgenstein, and read *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus*, Wittgenstein’s great book, before it was published. {041-R11} The two men served together in the First World War.
Varma once came across Wittgenstein’s wartime diaries on Twitter. You think of a great philosopher, he said, and wonder what he must be writing about in the trenches. {041-S04}

The answer was wanting sex. Varma admitted the detour was “completely unrelated” to Hayek’s paper, and returned to how Hayek got into Marxism at the London School of Economics before a book by Ludwig von Mises made him a classical liberal.

quote.text: And in the trenches, he is just basically writing about wanting to masturbate and wanting sex.

second.caption: Wittgenstein’s wartime diaries

third.head: The outsider’s Nobel
body: Ronald Coase was a law thinker, not even an economist, Ajay Shah said, and yet he won the Nobel Prize in Economics. {#coasenobel} Amit Varma cut in with the name of the show: “Everything is everything.”
Being an outsider, Shah argued, was an advantage. Coase did not take the economists’ vocabulary and modelling strategies for granted. “He curiously wondered why does this make sense.” {041-S07}
His puzzle sounded almost naive. Outside a firm, commerce runs on prices, bargains and contracts. Inside its boundary wall, nobody negotiates: there is an organisation chart, and people fall in line.

His answer, in 1937, was that contracting is costly. {041-C10} Deals take time, effort and emotional energy, and once signed they keep needing renegotiation as the world misbehaves. Inside a firm, the boss simply says what to do.
third.caption: the outsider who won the Nobel

p2.title: Paper trail
p2.deck: Three papers and an essay, from Friedman, Hayek, Coase and Bastiat, championed by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

sections.label: The first paper
sections.head: The people are not dumb
sections.caption: Friedman and the natural rate
body: John Maynard Keynes, Ajay Shah said, practically invented macroeconomics in the fires of the Great Depression. Before him, nobody meaningfully treated an economy as a unit of observation. {041-C01}

The Keynesian package that followed let government manage the business cycle, largely through fiscal policy, and relegated monetary policy to low importance. It did not take the people seriously, Shah said.
Through the 1960s the package came apart. In 1968 Milton Friedman became president of the American Economic Association, which gave him a platform for a speech. {#aea}

His central move, Shah said, was to treat people as optimisers: when government acts, they respond. “You can have some data set and you can fit a model, but you should not assume that those relationships are stable.” {041-C02}
## A floor for unemployment
Friedman also set out the natural rate of unemployment. Some people are always switching jobs, laid off or out of the labour force, so unemployment can never be driven to zero.

Monetary policy, in his framework, should preserve the value of the currency in a stable and predictable way, and not chase ambitious goals. A good central bank, Shah said later, is a simple utility that delivers an inflation target and does nothing else.

~ Shah added a second pillar. Friedman’s study of the Great Depression showed that when the banking system blows up, it can take the economy down with it. Ben Bernanke worked out the details, and was running the Fed in 2008. {041-C06}

quote.text: There is something below which it can’t really go without driving the inflation to hell.

sections.label: The second paper
sections.head: What the planner can’t know
sections.caption: Hayek and the knowledge problem
body: Friedrich Hayek’s essay came out in 1945 as a rebuttal to the economist Oscar Lange, who wanted a Central Pricing Board to set the price of everything. “CPB, lovely acronym,” Amit Varma noted. {041-J14}

Planners, Hayek argued, treat running an economy as a problem of logic: collect the data and apply the right rule. But knowledge is too dispersed to collect. “Sometimes even I do not know what my desires will be tomorrow,” Varma said. {041-C07}
He borrowed Ajay Shah’s example from their episode on power: on a cloudy day people switch off their air conditioners, and use them more at night. No one can predict such things.
## Order without orders

So how can someone in Mumbai coordinate with a trader in Ludhiana or a farmer in Bengal? Through prices. An earthquake disrupts a tin factory; you never hear of it, but the price of tin rises, and you economise.
Had prices been one person’s invention, Varma said, he would be ranked among the greatest thinkers in human history. Shah agreed. “It is nothing less than miraculous.” {041-C08}
~ Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok, Varma noted, have a line that almost sums up the essay: “a price is a signal wrapped in an incentive”.

quote.text: a lot of beautiful things in the world are the product of human action, but not human design.
quote.who: Adam Ferguson, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: The third paper
sections.head: Inside the firm, no haggling
sections.caption: why firms exist
body: Ajay Shah’s second paper was Ronald Coase’s 1937 article *The Nature of the Firm*. {041-R03} It opened his mind, he said, to thinking about the market economy, treating the firm not as a black box that maximises profit but as a complicated, messy thing to be understood.

Picture the market as atomic individuals, all bargaining and contracting, Shah said, with little fortresses of firms inside it. Contracting is costly, so within the fortress the boss says do this, and nobody haggles over the price.
That is efficient, but it gives up the flexibility of markets. The optimal size of a firm is where the trade-offs balance out.
## Firms after Coase

Amit Varma added that a firm’s autocracy is no case for autocratic rulers: you join voluntarily, sign a contract and can leave. Calling corporate work modern slavery, he said, gets it wrong. {041-C12}

As transaction costs change, Shah said, the firm should be rethought. Open-source software lets loose coalitions of individuals make what companies once made, without the burden of being inside a firm.
~ Nor need a firm be Stalinist. A company like Hindustan Lever has had many changes of chief executive without changing its character, Shah said, because power inside it is dispersed. {041-C11}

quote.text: And then the day the document is signed, the universe starts misbehaving and doing strange things.

sections.label: The essay
sections.head: Six francs and a missing shoe
sections.caption: the seen and the unseen
body: Frédéric Bastiat’s essay *That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen* is where Amit Varma got the name of his podcast. It begins with a stone through a window. {041-R04}

Onlookers give their gyan: the broken window is good for the economy, since the glazier will get six francs and money is moving. Bastiat, in Varma’s telling, borrows a phrase of Ajay Shah’s to reply: “Hey, Mr. Gas, keep quiet.” {041-J08}
What is seen is the glazier’s six francs. What is not seen is the shoe or the book the owner would have bought with them. {041-C13}
This, Varma said, is opportunity cost, described about sixty years before the term was coined. Bastiat applied it to taxes, state sponsorship of the arts and conscription.
## One game of Candy Crush

Varma teaches the essay in his writing course. You sit down to write, play one game of Candy Crush, and lose the hour. The dopamine hits are what is seen. “The opportunity cost is that you made your future self stupid,” he said. {041-C14}
~ He also recommended Bastiat’s *The Candlemaker’s Petition*, in which candlemakers ask the government to block the sun, and *The Law*, which he called a masterpiece.

quote.text: I look at Bastiat and I think that is a model public intellectual. That’s a Renaissance man.

side.boxText: Three papers and an essay: Friedman on monetary policy (1968), Hayek on knowledge (1945), Coase on the firm (1937) and Bastiat on the seen and the unseen. Ajay Shah calls Friedman’s the turning point of twentieth-century macroeconomics. {041-R01}

contQuote.text: What strikes me about this paper and all good economic work is the thinking behind it, that these are foundational principles, this is a frame you bring, this is how you think about something.

p3.deck: A speech, a dying vow, two lone warriors and a prize twice won

stories.caption: Friedman’s 1968 speech
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the 1968 speech that reset macroeconomics
stories.head: The speech that called the 1970s
body: In the 1950s, Ajay Shah said, Keynesian economists were confident they had licked the business cycle. The government would run big fiscal policy, manage the ups and downs, and that would be that.
Through the 1960s, that confidence came apart. A very famous Kennedy tax cut in 1964, backed by models and forecasts, was supposed to do certain things, and it did not really work. {#kennedy}

In 1968 Milton Friedman became president of the American Economic Association, and gave a speech. In it, Shah said, “he told a story”: what monetary policy can do, what it cannot, and how to think about such questions.
Para after para, Friedman played through how people would respond to government. He set out the natural rate of unemployment. And he wrote it in plain English.
Then the world obliged. For ten or fifteen years after the speech, old-style macro policy did not work very well, and the inflation of the seventies clicked with what he had said. {041-S01}

Robert Lucas and collaborators such as Tom Sargent and Ed Prescott then turned his ideas into simple, clean models that could be brought to the data. That, Shah said, has become “the entire machinery of modern economics”.

~ The trail ends in today’s central banks. All the sensible countries now run inflation targets, Shah said, and India got there in 2015, with a huge difference to the stability of its economy. {#india2015}
stories.why: A clearly argued idea, delivered just before events bear it out, can redirect a whole discipline, and later its institutions. Shah’s verdict: it was “a good speech at the right time and it came out right in hindsight”.
stories.postscript: Friedman’s 1968 version was about money supply. Central banks gave that up in the early 1980s and steer interest rates instead, Shah said. {041-J12}

stories.end: So deeply moving, but that's the kind of man that he was
stories.caption: Bastiat’s dying vow
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the life and death of a hero
stories.head: Principles to the last breath
body: Frédéric Bastiat, one of Amit Varma’s heroes, was born in 1801 and died in 1850 at the age of 49. He was a great essayist and, Varma thought, a member of parliament for some time. {#bastiatborn}
Bastiat did not stay at his desk. He travelled around popularising his work, and on a book tour in the US, Varma said, he caught tuberculosis. {041-S08}

Realising he was dying, Bastiat said something to the effect that he would scream out his principles with all the power in his lungs till his dying breath. “Tuberculosis lungs, right?” Varma said. “So deeply moving, but that’s the kind of man that he was.”
~ Varma marvels that Bastiat stated ideas that scholars formalised only decades later, in simple language that absolutely anyone could understand. “It blows my mind,” he said.
stories.why: Bastiat put ideas into plain words decades before scholars formalised them, and treated them as worth his last breath. People come and go, Varma said at the episode’s end; ideas shape civilisation. {041-C16}
stories.postscript: Varma first gave Bastiat’s birth year as 1799, then settled on 1801.

stories.start: It's time for some BTS. You know what is BTS?
stories.end: K. P. Krishnan and Ajay were like lone warriors in a sense.
stories.caption: the lone warriors of inflation targeting
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a decade-long fight for inflation targeting
stories.head: Nonsense, shouted on cue
body: Amit Varma interrupted the episode for some behind-the-scenes footage, or BTS. Someone off camera was coaxed into shouting at Ajay Shah: “Inflation targeting is nonsense.” {041-J01}
“You see what Ajay has to kind of go through,” Varma told viewers. Then he turned serious. {041-S02}
Shah, Varma said, was one of a handful of people fighting for inflation targeting a decade before it happened in India. He and K. P. Krishnan were “like lone warriors in a sense”.

~ India adopted the regime in 2015. Shah said it has made a huge difference in simplifying and stabilising the Indian economy, and Varma pointed viewers to his eight-hour episode with Krishnan, which tells the story in detail. “So congratulations for that,” he told Shah.
stories.why: Reforms that look obvious in hindsight often begin as lonely, mocked causes kept alive by a few. The cause here was a target: four per cent inflation, with the RBI held accountable for hitting it. {#target}

stories.end: go against conventional uh thinking. And I just love the man so much
stories.caption: the Bastiat Prize
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the award named after his hero
stories.head: Twice blessed by Bastiat
body: There used to be a global prize for journalism named after Frédéric Bastiat, Amit Varma said, given to writers who promote the free society. Varma won it twice, in 2007 and 2015. {041-S09}
The money was useful at the time, he said, and validation is always nice. But it meant a lot to him for another reason: the man the prize was named after.

Bastiat, in Varma’s eyes, was a Renaissance man with interests across everything and no credentialism. He had not been to a great university and was not part of the system, an outsider whose ideas went against conventional thinking. “I just love the man so much,” Varma said.
~ He thinks Tim Harford is the only other person to have won it twice.
stories.why: Being claimed by a tradition you admire can mean more than the money. Bastiat is Varma’s template for thinking without credentials, and his essay gave Varma’s podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, its name. {041-J15}

quiz.q: In Bastiat’s parable of the broken window, what is seen and what is not?
quiz.a: The glazier’s six francs; unseen is the shoe or book the owner forgoes.

quiz.q: What is the one thing a good central bank should do, in Ajay Shah’s view?
quiz.a: Control the short-term interest rate to deliver a stable, predictable inflation target.

quiz.q: Whose proposal for a Central Pricing Board was Hayek’s 1945 essay written to rebut?
quiz.a: The economist Oscar Lange, whom Varma urged listeners to ignore completely.

quiz.q: Why do firms exist at all, according to Ronald Coase’s 1937 article?
quiz.a: Because contracting is costly: bargaining, lawyering and renegotiation all take time and effort.

quiz.q: Which book turned the young Hayek from socialism into a classical liberal?
quiz.a: *Socialism*, by Ludwig von Mises, read after Hayek had drifted into Marxism at LSE.

quiz.q: Who stopped colleagues in university hallways to ask if they had read Hayek’s essay?
quiz.a: The economist Armen Alchian: “Have you read this? You have to read this.”
